name: Chutney

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Indo-Caribbean people created chutney around the 1940s, drawing on ancestral Bhojpuri folk music from the Hindi Belt.
British authorities brought these indentured labourers to replace enslaved workers on sugar plantations after 1838.
Early chutney originated from traditional wedding songs performed largely by women in Trinidad and Tobago and Suriname.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally rooted in Caribbean Hindu weddings and religious contexts, chutney later expanded to secular celebrations and major competitions like Trinidad Carnival.
It serves as a vital cultural unifier and identity marker for the Indo-Caribbean diaspora.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Chutney is an uptempo genre combining Indian classical and folk music, Bhojpuri folk, Hindi film music, calypso, and soca.
Key traditional instruments include the dholak drum, harmonium, and dhantal iron rod, later joined by bass guitars, synthesizers, drum machines, and tassa drums.
Listen for the dholak, dhantal, harmonium, bass guitar.

Chutney music features a fast, driving tempo driven by the acoustic rhythm of the dholak and dhantal, accompanied by the melodic lead of the harmonium and layered with modern bass guitars, synthesizers, and soca beats.

music_brief.purpose: original soundtrack faithful to the tradition, with documented commercial reuse rights and no recurring royalties
music_brief.rights_rule: A composition brief does not clear an output. Record the provider/model/version, terms and date, input rights, output licence, restrictions and review before release.
music_brief.rhythm_pattern: dholak beats mixed with soca beat
music_brief.vocal_style: sung in Caribbean English, Caribbean Hindustani, and Bhojpuri
music_brief.musical_form: fusion of traditional Indian songs over fast Caribbean beats
music_brief.sound_description: Chutney music features a fast, driving tempo driven by the acoustic rhythm of the dholak and dhantal, accompanied by the melodic lead of the harmonium and layered with modern bass guitars, synthesizers, and soca beats.
music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Chutney (Trinidad and Tobago). Rhythm pattern: dholak beats mixed with soca beat. Instruments: dholak, dhantal, harmonium, bass guitar, electric guitar, synthesizer, drum machine, tassa. Vocal style: sung in Caribbean English, Caribbean Hindustani, and Bhojpuri. Form: fusion of traditional Indian songs over fast Caribbean beats. Mood: uptempo, danceable, festive. It should sound like this: Chutney music features a fast, driving tempo driven by the acoustic rhythm of the dholak and dhantal, accompanied by the melodic lead of the harmonium and layered with modern bass guitars, synthesizers, and soca beats. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.

no caricature, no exaggeration, no mixing of regions or eras
